points.issue: Load-bearing claim for the scene: "A large context window, conversation history, images, tool output, or a RAG pipeline that stuffs retrieved documents into a prompt can push more bytes up than the final answer sends down." Grounded — supported. Modern LLM API request payloads (long context, base64 images, tool-call outputs, retrieved documents) can run into the tens of megabytes, while typical text completions are far smaller, so the upload-heavier-than-download framing holds for the RAG/long-context case the script describes.
points.suggested_fix: No factual correction needed; the claim is grounded. Optional: keep as-is.

grounded.source: Anthropic Claude API Reference, "Messages API" (request payload limits for conversation history, base64 images, tool outputs, and document blocks vs. typical output token response sizes)

points.issue: Claim: "Many home and office connections provide less upload capacity than download capacity" (asymmetric broadband). Grounded — supported. Cable, DSL, and many consumer fiber tiers are commonly provisioned with materially lower upload than download bandwidth.
points.suggested_fix: No factual correction needed; the claim is grounded. Optional: keep as-is.

points.issue: Claim: "Depending on the protocol, the data may travel over TCP protected by TLS, or over QUIC, which runs over UDP." Grounded — supported. This is the standard protocol layering described in the relevant IETF specifications.
points.suggested_fix: No factual correction needed; the claim is grounded. Optional: keep as-is.

grounded.source: IETF RFC 9000 (QUIC: A UDP-Based Multiplexed and Secure Transport); IETF RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3)

points.issue: Claim: at high concurrency, "session-table capacity, available ports, firewall limits, and idle timers become real resources. When they come under pressure, the symptom may be intermittent timeouts—not a neat alert." Grounded — supported. Vendor troubleshooting documentation for NAT/PAT port exhaustion describes exactly this symptom shape: silent, intermittent connection failures rather than a labeled error.
points.suggested_fix: No factual correction needed; the claim is grounded. Optional: keep as-is.

grounded.source: Microsoft Learn, "Troubleshoot intermittent outbound connection errors in Azure App Service"; AWS Documentation, "Monitor NAT gateways with Amazon CloudWatch" (ErrorPortAllocation metric)

points.issue: Claim: "Some services also use DNS answers as one input for steering clients toward an edge or region." Grounded — supported. Latency-based and geolocation DNS routing, plus GSLB, are documented, real mechanisms used by major cloud/CDN providers for exactly this purpose.
points.suggested_fix: No factual correction needed; the claim is grounded. Optional: keep as-is.

grounded.source: AWS Route 53 Developer Guide ("Choosing a routing policy" — latency-based and geolocation routing); Cloudflare GSLB documentation

points.issue: Claim: ISP routers "forward it using addresses, routing information, labels, traffic classes, and policy." Step 2 flagged "labels" as a possible overreach for a generic consumer ISP path (it implies MPLS). Grounded — supported that MPLS label-switching is a real, standard mechanism, but the grounding pass could not confirm it applies to every hop of a generic residential path specifically — MPLS is most reliably a backbone/provider-core technology, not necessarily present on the access/last-mile hop.
points.suggested_fix: Keep "labels" — it is accurate for the ISP backbone/core hops the scene is describing — but consider a light precision note (on-screen or narration) that label-switching applies deeper in the provider network rather than implying every hop uses it.

grounded.source: IETF RFC 3031 (Multiprotocol Label Switching Architecture); IETF RFC 4364 (BGP/MPLS IP VPNs)
grounded.note: Confirms MPLS label-switching is real and standard, but grounding did not establish it as universal on the access/last-mile hop specifically — it is most reliably a backbone/provider-core mechanism. Scene wording is broad enough ("the provider") that this is a minor scope nuance, not a correction.

points.issue: Claim: "BGP distributes reachability information between them and lets each organization apply routing policy. It does not simply draw the geographically shortest line between you and the cloud." Grounded — supported. BGP's decision process is policy-driven (AS path length, local preference, MEDs, etc.), not a shortest-physical-path algorithm.
points.suggested_fix: No factual correction needed; the claim is grounded. Optional: keep as-is.

grounded.source: IETF RFC 4271 (A Border Gateway Protocol 4 (BGP-4), Section 9.1, Decision Process)

points.issue: Claim: enterprise TLS inspection "terminates the encrypted connection, examines the decrypted content, and establishes a new encrypted connection onward," and "certificate pinning, privacy requirements, application design, or end-to-end encryption may prevent inspection or cause the connection to fail instead." Grounded — supported; this is the standard forward-proxy TLS-inspection mechanism, and pinning causing a hard connection failure (rather than silent bypass) matches documented behavior. Step 2 noted the same claim shape was previously grounded as supported for the prior (non-automated) project — this draft's phrasing is consistent with that finding.
points.suggested_fix: No factual correction needed; the claim is grounded. Optional: keep as-is.

grounded.source: Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS Administrator's Guide (SSL Forward Proxy Decryption; Certificate Pinning Issues in SSL Decryption)
